title: Serve one request from your own process
why: The browser is another process. The game server owns authoritative state and answers over HTTP.
outcome: Start a practice server, send one request, and diagnose a refused connection.

steps.title: Two processes, one contract
steps.question: Why does the game need a server process?
explanation: Browsers cannot be trusted with scores, hidden tests, or time. The server holds the Match record, checks membership and deadlines, and answers requests with JSON.

You need this now because every later screen calls this server. Reference preview: services/game/src/main.ts boots the Nest application and listens on a port. Your practice server starts smaller with plain HTTP and grows toward the same shape.

vocabulary.meaning: A separate process that owns Match state and answers HTTP requests.
A number naming one listening service on a machine.

hints: Answer: authority lives off-device.
Find the listen call.
Compare with a referee off the field.
Read the expected result before you change code.

steps.title: See client, port, JSON
steps.question: What travels each way?
explanation: Out: method, path, headers, body. Back: status code plus JSON. A refused connection means no process listens at that port.

Reference preview: services/game/src/main.ts creates the Nest application and listens (lines 1-13). Practice path: src/server/main.ts. Future team path: the real service module, mapped in M13.

steps.title: Name the server scripts
steps.question: Which commands start and check the server?
explanation: Two names: dev:server compiles and starts the API process; test:service runs the HTTP tests. Scripts live in package.json so every learner uses the same command.

Add dev:server as npm run build && node dist/src/server/main.js. Add test:service as vitest run test/http.test.ts. Vite is added in M07, so the server command works before the browser toolchain exists.

Analogous example: like the M01 scripts, each name is a short label for a command.
Walkthrough: edit only the scripts object, save package.json, then run npm pkg get scripts.

title: Route to the rules you already tested
why: Routes translate HTTP into calls to pure game behavior. The rules stay framework-free.
outcome: Wire a route to an existing pure rule with constructor injection.

steps.title: Thin routes, fat rules
steps.question: What may a route contain?
explanation: Parsing and delegation only. The route reads the path and body, then calls an already-tested rule or service. New logic in a route is a smell.
Dependency injection first means passing the service object into the route holder. Nest decorators automate the wiring later; the idea stays the same.

vocabulary.meaning: HTTP layer that parses requests and calls game behavior. Holds no game rules.

steps.title: Pass the service in
steps.question: What does constructor injection replace?
explanation: The first server made HTTP visible. Now replace its hand-written route with Nest, the framework used by the reference game service. A controller receives the request; a service calls the rule; a module registers both.
A decorator is a label beginning with @ that tells Nest what a class or method does. Constructor injection means Nest passes the registered service into the controller.

vocabulary.meaning: An @ label that tells Nest how to connect a class or method.
A Nest registration file that lists controllers and providers.

steps.title: Install Nest and enable its decorators
steps.question: Which settings let TypeScript understand Nest classes?
explanation: At the practice root, install the reference-locked server packages: npm install --save-exact @nestjs/common@11.2.6 @nestjs/core@11.2.6 @nestjs/platform-express@11.2.6 reflect-metadata@0.2.2 rxjs@7.8.2. Then add the reference-locked type package with npm install --save-dev --save-exact @types/express@4.17.25.

Edit tsconfig.json to add experimentalDecorators: true and emitDecoratorMetadata: true. These settings let TypeScript keep the class information Nest uses for injection. Keep the other M01 settings unchanged.

vocabulary.meaning: Extra information kept with a class so Nest can connect its dependencies.

hints: Goal: package.json lists five runtime packages and @types/express; tsconfig enables both decorator settings.
Relevant value: npm ls --depth=0 lists the installed versions; npm run typecheck still passes.
Analogous example: like adding a header before compiling C, the setting enables syntax the compiler otherwise rejects.
Walkthrough: install the runtime group, install the type package, edit only the two compiler options, then inspect the package list.

files.owner: The practice root owns its installed server tools.
files.change: Add the five exact runtime versions and the exact @types/express development version shown.
files.pattern: Use --save-exact so package.json records fixed versions.

steps.next: Create the module, controller, and service.

steps.title: Move the request into Nest
steps.question: Does the route call your tested rule?
explanation: Practice paths: create src/server/game.module.ts, game.controller.ts, and game.service.ts; edit main.ts and test/server.ts. The module registers the controller and service. The controller receives GameService and delegates to the M03 deadline rule. Use @Inject(GameService) on the constructor parameter: Vitest transforms source TypeScript without emitDecoratorMetadata, and the explicit token works in both tests and the built server. Add @HttpCode(200) to keep the same status as the plain HTTP route introduced one lesson earlier; Nest otherwise defaults POST to 201.
The service takes a small rule object in its constructor. The Nest module supplies the existing M03 rule with a provider factory; no deadline formula is copied into the controller.
hints: Goal: POST /practice-decision follows controller → injected service → existing deadline rule.
Relevant value: secondsLeft 12 and 0 return the existing rule answers.
Analogous example: like passing Judge into run(), pass the rule into the service once.

Walkthrough: register the provider factory in GameModule, mark the controller constructor parameter @Inject(GameService), bootstrap GameModule in main.ts, and start it through test/server.ts. Keep POST at 200 with @HttpCode(200).

title: Reject bad JSON with 400
why: TypeScript annotations vanish at runtime. The server must check untrusted bodies itself.
outcome: Validate one teaching route and return clear 400 errors.

steps.title: Annotations do not guard the network
steps.question: Why check a body TypeScript already types?
explanation: Annotations disappear when compiled. Any client can send a string where a number belongs. The route must verify shapes at runtime and answer 400 for bad input.
This teaching route is POST /practice-decision with {secondsLeft: number}. It does not authorize a game Submit; the gameplay controller later consumes trusted identity and authoritative Match time.

vocabulary.meaning: Runtime shape checking of untrusted input. Failures answer 400.

title: Attach a verified identity, not a body field
why: Membership needs a server-verified actor. Client-supplied player IDs are untrusted.
outcome: Reject missing, untrusted, and outsider actors before membership.

steps.title: Who says who you are?
steps.question: Why is a body playerId untrusted?
explanation: Anyone can type any name into a request body. The server attaches identity from a verified seam — here a development-only header adapter, later real authentication.
The practice adapter is conspicuously development-only: it reads x-dev-user-id only when explicitly enabled, and production replaces it without changing game logic.

vocabulary.meaning: Server-verified actor attached before membership. Never a body field.
